content: Intentional failure to supply products or the deliberate provision of substandard quality products can have significant implications for public health and safety. Ensuring the availability of high-quality medicines is critical to maintaining trust in healthcare systems and achieving optimal therapeutic outcomes. The promotion of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines is a key public health strategy. Generic medicines, also known as multisource pharmaceutical products, are pharmaceutically equivalent or alternative products to innovator medicines. When therapeutically equivalent, these products are interchangeable and must meet the same rigorous standards of quality, efficacy, and safety as the original innovator products. Branded generics are generic medicines marketed under a brand name by their manufacturers. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that countries adopt legislative and administrative measures to facilitate the early market entry of generic and biosimilar medicines. This includes encouraging the early submission of regulatory applications, ensuring prompt and effective review processes, and guaranteeing that these products meet stringent safety, efficacy, and quality standards. Governments have implemented a range of supplyand demand-side measures to promote the use of generic and biosimilar medicines. Supply-side measures include removing regulatory barriers, utilizing voluntary licensing agreements, applying WTO TRIPS flexibilities for patented medicines when appropriate, and implementing specific pricing and purchasing policies, such as internal reference pricing. Demand-side measures include preferential co-payment plans for generic medicines, mandatory substitution policies, and educational campaigns to raise awareness about the efficacy and safety of generic medicines. Similar policies have been applied to biosimilar medicines, albeit to a lesser extent. The use of quality-assured generic medicines has been a global public health priority since the 1990s. WHO strongly recommends that countries adopt multiple pricing policies to achieve low prices for generic and biosimilar medicines, informed by production costs. These policies may include internal reference pricing, mark-up regulation, tendering, and reduced patient co-payments. Educational programs for both consumers and healthcare professionals are also essential to address misconceptions about the quality, safety, and efficacy of generic and biosimilar medicines. The evidence supports the benefits of promoting quality-assured generic medicines, including reduced prices, improved equity, and enhanced financial sustainability of healthcare systems. However, challenges remain, particularly in low-income countries where regulatory capacity may be limited, and reliance on third-party quality control laboratories may be necessary. Addressing these challenges requires clear legislation, national guidelines on substitution, and education for clinicians and pharmacy personnel. Pooled procurement of medicines is another strategy to improve access and affordability. This involves collective purchasing arrangements that leverage economies of scale to reduce prices and streamline procurement processes. WHO suggests that pooled procurement should be accompanied by transparent processes, strong governance, and sustainable financing mechanisms. Successful examples of pooled procurement include initiatives for HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria medicines in low-income countries, as well as regional and international collaborations. The feasibility and sustainability of pooled procurement depend on harmonized legal, regulatory, and administrative frameworks, as well as political commitment and alignment of processes. Long-standing pooled procurement mechanisms demonstrate that such arrangements can be financially sustainable in the long term, provided that initial resource requirements and integration challenges are addressed effectively. In summary, promoting the use of quality-assured generic and biosimilar medicines, alongside pooled procurement strategies, can enhance access, affordability, and equity in healthcare. These policies require careful design, implementation, and monitoring to ensure their effectiveness and sustainability in diverse healthcare contexts.
